uses.sentence: He never broke communion over it.
uses.paragraph: Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.
uses.record_text:
We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

use_note.means: Donatists claimed their rebaptism continued the African ruling of Cyprian's council of 256, not an unbroken apostolic custom.
not_for: a claim that Donatists asserted an apostolic pedigree for their practice
a claim that Cyprian broke communion over rebaptism

uses.sentence: A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over.
uses.paragraph: The step itself is the washing. That is not a threshold you clear before belonging. It is the entry. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.
uses.record_text: We do not think of this as baptizing twice. Nothing happened the first time. A hand from a tainted line washes nothing. So when someone comes to us from the other church, we give the first real baptism they have had.

use_note.means: For Donatists it was no second baptism: a hand from a tainted line washes nothing, so those from the other church received their first real one.
not_for: a claim that it was a modern adult rebaptism chosen for personal renewal
a claim that it was a ritual scruple about repeating a sacrament
a claim that it denied the first rite happened at all, rather than that it conferred anything
a claim that it was a private opinion of a rigorist minority rather than the communion's enacted norm

uses.sentence: We are the church that says a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and that is what our founding generation was doing with an accusation it believed.
uses.paragraph: And there was worse. In the year 320 an official put our own people on oath about where four hundred pieces of silver had gone, and read our bishops' letters into the record. One had written to another urging him to settle a charge quietly, before the flame burst out — and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that says a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and that is what our founding generation was doing with an accusation it believed.
uses.record_text:
Yes, and we can hand you the transcript.

In the year 320 an official put our own people on oath about where four hundred pieces of silver had gone, and read our bishops' letters into the record. One of them wrote to another urging him to settle a charge quietly, before the flame burst out - and said in the same letter that he knew the accusation was true. Another wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. A deacon who had been degraded made the complaint, and a witness testified that the people of the town had shouted against making that man bishop in the first place, and that he had been a betrayer. We are the church that says a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and that is what our founding generation was doing with an accusation it believed.

Now defend the second thing. We cannot, and we will not try. When our own council at Bagai condemned the breakaway party, and then decided to take two of its bishops back, a general came with soldiers and enforced the reconciliation. When the same party would not be dislodged, we went to the imperial and proconsular authorities and used the law against heretics on them - the very law and the very machinery we spent a century saying had no standing to judge the church. Not one page survives of anyone on our side explaining how those two things go together. We are not going to invent the page. What we will not accept is being told this was hidden: it was not. It sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where our doctrine is at its hardest.

It reached further down than councils and generals, too. The same opponent who lists our worst episodes names a leader of ours, Faustinus, who at Hippo ordered that no one should bake bread for Catholics, "in consequence of the scanty numbers of the Catholics in the place." A baker - an ordinary man, the tenant of one of the other side's own deacons - did as he was told and threw away his own landlord's bread unbaked, and that deacon was, in the telling, cut off from what he needed "not only in a Roman state, but even in his own country, and not only in his own country, but in his own house." We do not know the baker's name, his reasons, or what became of him afterward, and we will not supply them. What the story shows, if it is true as told, is that this fight reached into an actual bakehouse and an actual household, carried out by someone with no office at all.

Our country members are said to have attacked the other side's clergy and forced washings on people. That they existed and were legislated against we know from imperial law. What they actually did comes almost entirely from people writing to make them look like a mob, and we will not repeat that portrait as though it were a police report, or deny it as though we had a better one.

The temples, and what became of the old gods once Christians had the power - that was never our question to answer. We never held that kind of power. The state was against us for nearly our whole existence, and nothing survives of what we did about the old religion in the regions where we were the church of everyone. We would be guessing, and you would not be able to tell.

use_note.means: Donatist bishops hushed a true charge, and the movement used troops and anti-heretical law against its own breakaway party.
not_for: a claim about the Donatists' own reasoning for the Bagai reception or the appeal to anti-heretical law
a claim that the polemical portrait of Circumcellion conduct is established fact
a claim about the baker's name, motive or fate
a claim about what the Donatists did to pagan temples

uses.sentence: Then the record simply stops.
uses.paragraph: No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.
uses.record_text:
Catholic means universal, and yes - we claimed it, and refused to hand it over. Both churches in every African town claimed it. What settled the usage was not an argument; it was the law. The emperor's officials attached the word to the other party and went on attaching it, and you can watch that happen in the transcript of our own trial. Our bishop told the judge that before the case is decided the name is an empty one, and that whoever is found to be a Christian will hold it at the end. The judge agreed - it is certain, he said, that after the contest the name belongs to those with whom the truth is found - and then said he was bound to follow the imperial rescript, which had already been pleased to call them by it. He conceded the principle and was not free to act on it. So we called them Caecilianists instead, after the man whose consecration we would not accept, and one of our preachers turned their own word back on them, saying it named the place where wrong is done and nobody is punished for it.

Is there a church today you could go and visit that is ours? No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

Denominations, in your sense - separate bodies agreeing to differ - we did not have and could not have had. There was one church, and the only question was which building held it. When a party broke from us, we did not treat it as another denomination. We condemned it in a council of three hundred and ten bishops, suppressed it, and then took two of its bishops back without redoing anything. When one man among us would not stop preaching that the church was spread over the whole earth, we cut him off and never received him back. That is what we did with people who called on Christ differently from us: not co-existence, and not quite consistency either.

use_note.means: Both African churches claimed the name catholic; imperial law gave it to the rival, and no traceable line of the Donatists survives today.
not_for: a claim that any present-day church descends from the Donatists
a claim that the absence of a documented descendant proves nothing survived
a claim that the pun on catholicus is attested beyond a modern editor's annotation
a claim that the Donatists treated rival bodies as parallel denominations

uses.sentence: We were not a small circle of the learned.
uses.paragraph: We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on - no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

uses.sentence: Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was.
uses.paragraph: It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was. Washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose. From 311 forward, through the great Conference at Carthage in 411, this was our established pattern. Two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs in that room, refusing the chairs offered because Christ stood before his own governor, and the washing was the one act that had made two churches out of one.
uses.record_text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You asked about prayer, the meal, and fasting, and here we have to thin out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

use_note.means: Entry meant being washed on coming from the rival communion, counted as a first baptism, while discipline for wrongdoing followed no consistent rule.
not_for: a claim about what undergoing the washing felt like to those who underwent it
a claim that a Donatist liturgy, order of service, or rule of fasting survives
a claim about the particulars of the forced-entry charges
a claim that a surviving rule explains why some condemned clergy were received back and others not

uses.sentence: We say for the first time.
uses.paragraph: We would, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. If you came to us from the other communion, you had already been through water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there. We held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt – so our own bishop wrote. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.
uses.record_text:
Born again - yes, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. If you came to us from the other communion you had already been through the water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there, and we held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless, our own bishop wrote, receives not faith but guilt. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.

And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. Whole imperial edicts were written against that single act, which is a strange kind of compliment: the state understood perfectly well that it was the one thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.

Babies, or only adults choosing for themselves? We cannot tell you, and we would rather admit it than round the answer off. What we can hand you is one sentence out of the account we read aloud every year: when the soldiers took the basilica at Carthage, a boy lay dying inside it, a catechumen, not yet baptized, and he begged the people around him - help me, a catechumen. That tells you the young were among us unbaptized and waiting. It does not tell you whether infants were washed. We will not build a practice out of one dying boy.

Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Nothing survives. Money moved among us - a wealthy woman's silver bought a consecration, a bishop left the church's whole treasury with laymen and an inventory with an old woman, a fuller paid twenty pieces to be made a priest - but every one of those reaches you out of a corruption inquiry, and none of it is a rule about giving.

The end of the world we cannot speak to at all. One man among us is reported to have expounded the Apocalypse entire, taking nothing in it in a bodily sense. He is the man our own council condemned, that commentary is not among the things this telling has read, and it would be dishonest to make him our voice on the last things when we would not let him speak on anything else.

use_note.means: Donatists counted the washing of those coming from the rival communion as a first baptism, a public act imperial law targeted.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists baptized infants, or that they did not
a claim about Donatist rules of giving or tithing
a claim about Donatist teaching on the end of the world

uses.sentence: The boundary we drew ran straight through the middle of the church, not around it — between our bishops and theirs, our font and theirs, our basilicas and theirs.
uses.paragraph: We never wrote that down. Not once. What we argued, for a century, was one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. The boundary we drew ran straight through the middle of the church, not around it — between our bishops and theirs, our font and theirs, our basilicas and theirs. Two hundred and seventy-nine of ours sat facing two hundred and eighty-six of theirs in one room, both sides reciting the same creed, and the whole fight was about which of the two communions was the true one. That is where our energy went. Not on the fate of pagans or the unbaptized, but on whether a man baptized by the other party's bishop had been baptized at all.
uses.record_text: Where our rival has a bishop, so do we. Two men claim one office over one city. It is a whole church order, see for see, across Roman North Africa. At the great Conference at Carthage, 279 of our bishops sat facing 286 of theirs.

use_note.means: Donatists had a bishop wherever their rival did, see for see across North Africa; at the 411 Conference 279 of theirs faced 286.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists were a loose protest movement without institutional structure
a claim that there was a single settled bishop of a city whom nobody contested
a claim that the rival claimant was understood by all sides to be irregular or provisional

uses.sentence: Every council our own bishops sat in was about one question, which was who the true church is, and none of them was about who Christ is.
uses.paragraph: So if you are asking whether we confessed Jesus as fully God, the answer is yes - but we were not the ones who worked that claim out. The great eastern councils of the fourth century do not appear in our record. Every council our own bishops sat in was about one question, which was who the true church is, and none of them was about who Christ is. We received the confession. We did not produce it.
uses.record_text:
A council of bishops decided, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in one sentence, and the same body later took two of the condemned back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.

You can check almost all of it, which is rarer than you think. The proceedings survive - the acts of the council at Cirta, the sentences from Cebarsussi and Bagai, and above all the transcript of the great conference at Carthage, where an imperial notary took down every word for three days. Read that one and you will see how we thought a case ought to be handled: our own bishop of Caesarea would not let the court touch the merits until it had settled, in order, the day, the mandate, the persons, and only then the cause. First find out who is in the room and by what warrant. Then argue.

What we would not accept was a council convened and enforced by a power that had already picked a side. Constantine's hearing at Rome ruled against us; so did the bishops at Arles. We rejected both, and not because a council cannot rule. A council whose venue, whose rules and whose enforcement all belong to a state that has already named the other party the Catholic church is not the church judging itself. That same thing happened again in front of us at Carthage: the judge agreed out loud that the name Catholic ought to follow the truth, and then said he was bound by the imperial rescript that had already awarded it. He conceded the principle and was not free to act on it.

And no, no council voted Jesus into being God. Not among us. The great eastern councils of that century are not our fight and do not appear in our record; every council our own bishops sat in was about one question, which was who the true church is, and none of them was about who Christ is. What we would say is narrower and worse: councils in our own day were used to settle which church the law would recognise, and we knew from the inside how much that decision owed to who had the emperor's ear.

use_note.means: Donatist councils of bishops decided disputes with real force, and Donatists rejected rulings convened and enforced by a state favouring their rival.
not_for: a claim that Donatist conciliar acta survive on their own terms
a claim that any Donatist council ruled on who Christ is
a claim that the surviving council documents are free of opponents' selection

uses.sentence: Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.
uses.paragraph: What belonging cost is not one thing, and we can put figures on part of it. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives. And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.
uses.record_text:
It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. If you are far from everyone you love, that is what we would have offered you - not a feeling of connection, but a date, and a thing that happens on it whether you are there or not.

use_note.means: Belonging cost confiscation, exile, graded fines and sometimes death, while councils, letters and fixed commemorations held Donatists together.
not_for: a claim that Donatist households were documented as split by the schism
a claim that the legal record shows personal or family costs
a claim resting on the commemorative sermon's family grief as a certified translation

uses.sentence: On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones elsewhere, someone carved *Deo laudes* — Praise to God.
uses.paragraph: On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones elsewhere, someone carved *Deo laudes* — Praise to God. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room.
uses.record_text:
A historian would ask you one question about everything we have told you, and it is the right question: who wrote it down? The answer, for nearly all of it, is our enemies. Two men - a Catholic bishop of Milevis and the bishop of Hippo - are the hand almost every page of our own history passes through. Our best theologian's letters survive chopped into clauses inside the book written to demolish them. The fullest account of our founding decade is a polemic aimed at proving us wrong. When you hear us tell a story with rich detail, ask first whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow.

Four things escape that, and only four, and each is short. A sermon preached at a martyr's grave. A passion of one of our bishops. One bishop's own letter to his own congregation. And one book of interpretation by a man our own council condemned. Add to that the transcript of the great conference, where a notary took our bishops down verbatim with no adversary choosing which words to keep - and note that the copy of it we can actually reach is the worst-damaged text in this whole corpus.

There is one thing nobody mediated at all. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our voice with no enemy between you and it, and it is two words long. We know our own shout better than we know the room we shouted it in.

Is it legend, then? Some of it will not stand as reporting, and we would not ask you to take it as reporting - our martyr accounts show visions, an unbroken body, a light on a hillside, and they were written to be read aloud at a graveside, not filed with a magistrate. But the founding documents run the other way, and they do not flatter us. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation, and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. We could not remove those if we wanted to. They are the most checkable things we have.

Where is our record thinnest? Wherever it could be checked without a hostile hand. The inner life of any ordinary member. The words of any woman among us. The rooms we met in. Our own account of any of the councils that judged us. And a whole shelf of modern work on us that this telling has not read.

use_note.means: Almost everything known of the Donatists was written by opponents; only a few texts and one two-word inscription speak as them.
not_for: a claim that the martyr accounts should be weighed as reporting
a claim that this self-assessment stands outside the corpus it describes
a claim that the silence of ordinary members is a thin margin of the record

uses.sentence: We watched it fail to.
uses.paragraph: There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge — wheat and tares against the world that does not know him — and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.
uses.record_text:
No, and the evidence for that is what our opponents had to say to beat us. Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge - wheat and tares against the world that does not know him - and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Genesis as a question about how the world was made - no. We have to tell you that nothing survives from us on it at all. That was not our fight, and we will not invent a position in it.

use_note.means: The Donatist case stood on the African precedent of Cyprian's council as well as on scripture, which alone never settled the dispute.
not_for: a claim that a Donatist statement on the authority of scripture survives
a claim about how the Donatists read Genesis or the making of the world

uses.sentence: Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other.
uses.paragraph: We held what our rivals held, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we confessed it as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.
uses.record_text:
Yes. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing - whose hand may give what the church gives - and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

Your third we would not have understood at all. My personal Lord and Savior - the words are yours and not ours, and they carry a whole way of being a Christian we did not have: one person, deciding privately, for himself. Ours was the opposite motion. You were baptized into a body, by named hands, in a town where everyone could see which building you walked into. If you had asked one of us whether Christ was his personally, he would probably have answered by telling you whose church he belonged to. He would not have been changing the subject. To us that was the subject.

use_note.means: Donatists confessed the same Trinitarian faith as their Catholic rivals; the dispute was over who could rightly give the sacraments.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists were heretics or held a different creed
a claim about Donatist teaching on substitutionary atonement, for or against
a claim that a Donatist creed survives as a separate document
a claim that Donatists understood faith as a personal, private decision

uses.sentence: Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver.
uses.paragraph: We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. The nearest we can bring you is small. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about what the person coming carries with them.
uses.record_text: What we look for is the conscience of the giver - the one who gives in holiness - to cleanse that of the recipient. Someone who knowingly takes faith from the faithless receives not faith, but guilt.

use_note.means: Petilian held that the giver's holy conscience is what cleanses the recipient, so faith knowingly taken from the faithless brings guilt instead.
not_for: a claim that validity turned on the minister's private, subjective sincerity
a claim that these words survive in a Donatist text rather than inside Augustine's refutation
a claim about Augustine's counter-argument

uses.sentence: The office was not honorary; the primate's rulings had real disciplinary force, and a council of bishops could depose or restore him.
uses.paragraph: Leadership among us ran through bishops and through councils — and the two held each other. A bishop could not simply decide for himself what the church was; three hundred and ten of them met at Bagai in one year and ruled as a body. Our senior bishop sat at Carthage — Donatus, then Parmenian, then Primian — while the rival claimed the same chair at the same time. So there were two primates in one city, as there were two bishops in every town. The office was not honorary; the primate's rulings had real disciplinary force, and a council of bishops could depose or restore him.
uses.record_text: Our senior bishop sits at Carthage. Donatus held it, then Parmenian, then Primian. Our rival claims the same see for its own man at the same time. So there are two primates in one city, as there are two bishops in every town.

uses.paragraph: Who held authority among us, and by what warrant? Bishops, and councils of bishops. That is the short answer and the most important one. We were not a loose association of the aggrieved. We built a complete rival church. Every see our rival claimed, we claimed too, bishop against bishop, down to towns you have never heard of. At Carthage itself our own primate sat opposite theirs, and when an imperial officer counted heads at the great conference in 411, two hundred and seventy-nine of our bishops stood up to be named.

uses.sentence: Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did.
uses.paragraph: Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.
uses.record_text:
We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

use_note.means: Donatists claimed their rebaptism continued the African ruling of Cyprian's council of 256, not an unbroken apostolic custom.
not_for: a claim that Donatists asserted an apostolic pedigree for their practice
a claim that Cyprian broke communion over rebaptism

uses.sentence: No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.
uses.paragraph: No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.
uses.record_text:
Bishops held authority, and councils held the bishops. That is the short answer, and the size of it is the part people get wrong. In the summer of 411 an imperial officer had both communions counted in one room, and the roll was read name by name: two hundred and seventy-nine of ours stood up, against two hundred and eighty-six of theirs. That is not a movement. That is one whole church facing another whole church, see for see, down to towns you have never heard of.

How did a man come to hold it? Both together: the people and the bishops. We can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back - let it be another; hear us, God - and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.

We would rather you did not hear "spread so far, so fast" about us at all, because that is not what happened. We did not travel out and win Africa. The split ran straight down through a church already there. In Numidia we were not the minority meeting quietly; we were simply the church of the village, and the other party was the newcomer. Our own councils were large enough to be governments: three hundred and ten bishops met at Bagai in one year, condemned a rival primate, and later received two of his bishops back.

What happened when we gathered? Less survives than you would think. We know the sound of it: where the other church said thanks to God, we said praise to God, and we cut those two words into stone near Bagai where anyone could read them. We know one day of the year in detail - the day we stood at a martyr's grave and heard the account of the death read out again. And we know what a gathering looked like when it was interrupted, because we read that aloud too: people on their knees with their eyes closed, clubbed where they knelt. Of the ordinary Sunday between those things, we have almost nothing.

Was it dangerous? Not as a daily terror; as a standing condition. Every see we held was held under law that did not recognise it. Basilicas were confiscated, clergy exiled, our country members fined by name in imperial legislation, and every so often the pressure came to a point and troops arrived. You did not live afraid every morning. You lived knowing it could tip, because it had.

use_note.means: Donatists formed a complete rival hierarchy of bishops and councils under standing legal jeopardy, and in Numidia were the ordinary church.
not_for: a claim about an ordinary Donatist service, as no liturgical text survives
a claim that a Donatist procedural rule for making bishops survives
a claim that imperial law confirms the polemical character given to the Circumcellions
a claim that the Donatists spread across Africa by mission

uses.sentence: Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies could not find burial — and then took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again.
uses.paragraph: And the door was wider than our reputation. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies could not find burial — and then took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Whatever else that tells you about us, it tells you the line was not always where our hardest language put it.
uses.record_text: Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemn a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot even find burial - and then take two of the condemned bishops back into office without rebaptizing or reordaining either one.

use_note.means: In 394 the Bagai council condemned the Maximianists as shipwrecked, unburied bodies; later two condemned bishops were taken back without rebaptism or reordination.
not_for: a claim that the episode simply exposes the rigorists as no better than anyone else
a claim that the exception was hidden

uses.sentence: After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon says that running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children.
uses.paragraph: We know families split over exactly that choice, because we read it aloud every year. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon says that running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading. The fight reached into households, not just between them.
uses.record_text: Every twelfth of March we read aloud the account of a day soldiers took a basilica at Carthage in the name of unity, and killed people at prayer inside it.

use_note.means: Every twelfth of March the community heard the sermon's account of soldiers seizing a Carthage basilica in the name of unity and killing worshippers inside.
not_for: a claim that the account comes from an inquest or a contemporary report
a claim that the preacher or the sermon's date is firmly established
a claim that any independent record of the deaths survives

uses.sentence: We would, and we would fight you over the arithmetic.
uses.paragraph: We would, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. If you came to us from the other communion, you had already been through water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there. We held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt – so our own bishop wrote. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.
uses.record_text:
Born again - yes, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. If you came to us from the other communion you had already been through the water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there, and we held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless, our own bishop wrote, receives not faith but guilt. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.

And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. Whole imperial edicts were written against that single act, which is a strange kind of compliment: the state understood perfectly well that it was the one thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.

Babies, or only adults choosing for themselves? We cannot tell you, and we would rather admit it than round the answer off. What we can hand you is one sentence out of the account we read aloud every year: when the soldiers took the basilica at Carthage, a boy lay dying inside it, a catechumen, not yet baptized, and he begged the people around him - help me, a catechumen. That tells you the young were among us unbaptized and waiting. It does not tell you whether infants were washed. We will not build a practice out of one dying boy.

Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Nothing survives. Money moved among us - a wealthy woman's silver bought a consecration, a bishop left the church's whole treasury with laymen and an inventory with an old woman, a fuller paid twenty pieces to be made a priest - but every one of those reaches you out of a corruption inquiry, and none of it is a rule about giving.

The end of the world we cannot speak to at all. One man among us is reported to have expounded the Apocalypse entire, taking nothing in it in a bodily sense. He is the man our own council condemned, that commentary is not among the things this telling has read, and it would be dishonest to make him our voice on the last things when we would not let him speak on anything else.

use_note.means: Donatists counted the washing of those coming from the rival communion as a first baptism, a public act imperial law targeted.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists baptized infants, or that they did not
a claim about Donatist rules of giving or tithing
a claim about Donatist teaching on the end of the world

uses.sentence: What survived is what we did with it.
uses.paragraph: As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.
uses.record_text:
What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

use_note.means: The Donatists traced themselves to the surrender of scripture under persecution and claimed descent through Cyprian's Carthage, not Rome.
not_for: a claim about how the Donatists argued for the resurrection
a claim that the Donatists appealed to eyewitness memory of Jesus
a claim that the Abitinian martyr acts are cleanly Donatist
a claim that the Donatist founding narrative reaches us unframed by an opponent

uses.sentence: We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside.
uses.paragraph: What we can show you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific than you may expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians — at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.
uses.record_text:
Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians - at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it.

Is Christianity one way among many? That question was not where our energy went, and we would only be guessing if we told you our view of it. What we can tell you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently - and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.

Did we think outsiders were going to hell? We will not put words in our own mouths. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt - which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

Divorce and remarriage we cannot speak to at all. There is nothing. Whether someone divorced could belong among us, or marry again, and on what terms - not a line survives, and we would rather leave the space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

use_note.means: Donatist exclusivity was aimed at the rival Christian communion and its sacraments, not at people outside the faith.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists taught those baptized by the other party were damned
a claim about Donatist views on whether Christianity is one way among many
a claim about Donatist teaching on divorce and remarriage

uses.sentence: His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it.
uses.paragraph: His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff — shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.
uses.record_text:
Start with the part that will surprise you: on Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit - and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. A church is not known by whose favour it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the Scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff - shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

use_note.means: Donatists shared their rivals' faith about Christ; at the 411 conference their bishops invoked Christ standing condemned before the governor.
not_for: a claim that a Donatist christological or soteriological treatise survives
a claim resting on the exact wording of Donatist bishops at the 411 conference
a claim that the Donatists held a distinct doctrine of Christ

uses.sentence: We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.
uses.paragraph: Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here — they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong. What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. One of our own bishops, asked at Carthage whether his own see still had a bishop in it, answered: through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way. Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing — but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.
uses.record_text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

use_note.means: The Donatists traced themselves to the surrender of scripture under persecution and claimed descent through Cyprian's Carthage, not Rome.

a claim that the Donatists appealed to eyewitness memory of Jesus
a claim that the Abitinian martyr acts are cleanly Donatist

uses.sentence: There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true.
uses.paragraph: What survives best is what opponents needed to argue against in detail: the purity doctrine itself, the legal and institutional shape of the schism, and the conciliar and imperial documentary record. When you hear us describe our founding dispute, the traditio accusation, or the great conference at Carthage, you are hearing what was preserved because it had to be answered. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation – and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. Those are the most checkable things we have, and they are the worst things about us.
uses.record_text:
A historian would ask you one question about everything we have told you, and it is the right question: who wrote it down? The answer, for nearly all of it, is our enemies. Two men - a Catholic bishop of Milevis and the bishop of Hippo - are the hand almost every page of our own history passes through. Our best theologian's letters survive chopped into clauses inside the book written to demolish them. The fullest account of our founding decade is a polemic aimed at proving us wrong. When you hear us tell a story with rich detail, ask first whether the detail is ours or the detail of a man who needed it to land a blow.

Four things escape that, and only four, and each is short. A sermon preached at a martyr's grave. A passion of one of our bishops. One bishop's own letter to his own congregation. And one book of interpretation by a man our own council condemned. Add to that the transcript of the great conference, where a notary took our bishops down verbatim with no adversary choosing which words to keep - and note that the copy of it we can actually reach is the worst-damaged text in this whole corpus.

There is one thing nobody mediated at all. On two pillars near Bagai, and on three other stones, two words are cut: Deo laudes. Praise to God. That is our voice with no enemy between you and it, and it is two words long. We know our own shout better than we know the room we shouted it in.

Is it legend, then? Some of it will not stand as reporting, and we would not ask you to take it as reporting - our martyr accounts show visions, an unbroken body, a light on a hillside, and they were written to be read aloud at a graveside, not filed with a magistrate. But the founding documents run the other way, and they do not flatter us. There is a court transcript in which a notary confesses, under threat of torture, that he forged the letter proving our central accusation, and that he did it working for our side. There is another in which our own bishops are read out advising each other, in writing, to keep a charge out of court because it was true. We could not remove those if we wanted to. They are the most checkable things we have.

Where is our record thinnest? Wherever it could be checked without a hostile hand. The inner life of any ordinary member. The words of any woman among us. The rooms we met in. Our own account of any of the councils that judged us. And a whole shelf of modern work on us that this telling has not read.

uses.sentence: We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over.
uses.paragraph: We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. The nearest we can bring you is small. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about what the person coming carries with them.
uses.record_text: You have asked us three questions we never argued. That will sound like dodging. It is not. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing. Whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works. The nearest we can bring you is small. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about the bread. Take those two and you have all we can honestly hand you. Anything more would be us making it up in a voice that sounds like ours.

uses.sentence: Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again.
uses.paragraph: And there is a second authority we cannot separate from the first: the martyrs themselves. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway. A bishop wrote to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death, whose bodies the proconsul sank in the sea so no one could venerate them — and the sea gave them back. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them. Scripture told us what the church is. The martyrs showed us.
uses.record_text:
Before anything about how we read them: notice what they were. Objects. Heavy ones. A magistrate could demand that a bishop carry them out of a building and hand them over, and some bishops did, and the whole of us exists because of that. No other church in the empire had its scriptures turn into the exact thing that split it.

How did we read them? Combatively, and about one subject. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse - the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. That is our reading in one exchange. We went to the text for a test of which of two visible churches was the true one, and we found the church described as the party the world hates rather than the party it favours.

We will not pretend that was a method. It was not. One man among us built an actual system for reading - seven rules, worked out and written down - and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

Which books did we treat as scripture? We cannot give you a list. Nothing that survives from us settles it, and we would rather say so than hand you the canon of some other church and put our name on it.

How did someone who could not read receive any of it? By standing still and listening, on a fixed day, in a particular place. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

use_note.means: Scripture was first a surrendered object, was read combatively to identify the true church, and reached most believers by being heard aloud.
not_for: a claim about which books the Donatists counted as scripture

uses.sentence: Two words could carry all of this.
uses.paragraph: You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God. Deo laudes. We cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that. Not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.
uses.record_text:
What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

not_for: a claim about the whole community's habit of reading beyond the one 411 exchange

Not one report of a Numidian church building is named anywhere in our own list of sources. There is no excavator, no site, no plan, no floor. What we do have is four stones. On two pillars near Bagai, twice over, someone cut two words: Deo laudes. Praise to God. Three more stones elsewhere carry the same words. That is the whole of what survives that you could touch. It is enough to prove we were there and what we shouted. It is not enough to show you a font, an altar, a doorway, or a room. We know our own shout better than the place we shouted it in. And if you ask how anyone knows our daily life at all, the answer is that mostly they do not. What they have is our enemies' books, one court transcript, four martyr texts, and the emperor's law. Every one of those is paper. None of it is a room.

uses.sentence: So authority among us was exercised as much in hushing things as in settling them, and we would not pretend that was rare.
uses.paragraph: The authority a bishop carried was real, but it was not absolute. When a charge came against one of our bishops, others among our own leadership wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out — and one of those letters admits the accusation was true. They wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way: let no one learn of it. So authority among us was exercised as much in hushing things as in settling them, and we would not pretend that was rare.
uses.record_text:
Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show.
