uses.sentence: It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives.
uses.paragraph: We have asked us a question we never argued. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing: whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works.
uses.record_text: You have asked us three questions we never argued. That will sound like dodging. It is not. We held one creed with the church we fought, word for word, and the split was never about God or grace or the bread. It was about one thing. Whose hand may give what the church gives. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. So we wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works. The nearest we can bring you is small. A rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took the cup, and a deacon told her off for it, and that is how we know we had a cup at all. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about the bread. Take those two and you have all we can honestly hand you. Anything more would be us making it up in a voice that sounds like ours.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

uses.sentence: Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days.
uses.paragraph: If you are asking what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.
uses.record_text:
Start with the part that will surprise you: on Christ himself we said what our opponents said. Word for word, creed for creed. Nobody in Africa called the other side heretics, because nobody could. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about who may hand on what he gave.

But if you ask what of him we kept nearest, we can tell you, because the answer shows up wherever our own people are allowed to speak at length. When an imperial judge sat down at Carthage and courteously offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit - and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and our bishops stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one who was tried by lawful authority and lost the case, and was right.

The good news, as we told it, ran along the same line. A church is not known by whose favour it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage finally reached the Scriptures, our own bishop of Caesarea answered verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. Read that in a town with two bishops and an emperor backing one of them, and it is not a devotional sentiment. It is a test, and we thought we could pass it.

His death meant that the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. Our own martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm four days before he was thrown from a cliff - shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. And a bishop writing to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death closed by telling them plainly that the same might yet be asked of any of them. That is our gospel in its working form: he stood, he was condemned, he was raised, and the day they come for you is not the day it all went wrong.

uses.paragraph: The smaller ledger we cannot give you. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. If you are far from everyone you love, that is what we would have offered you - not a feeling of connection, but a date, and a thing that happens on it whether you are there or not.

uses.sentence: Now think about what that telling costs the man making it.
uses.paragraph: Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage — her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it. The accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence. There was a second woman too, behind the later breakaway, whom the same hand parallels to her and never names at all. We can point you to no office a woman held among us, no council seat, no ordination — not because we are refusing you one, but because a hostile account of a rich woman's anger is the whole of what came down.
uses.record_text:
Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. It is what our people said to each other, in a letter, to readers who were likely to be next - and you should hear it as that, and not as a teaching about suffering that we ever worked out.

uses.sentence: Whether a marriage between our own and the rival communion was even recognized as a marriage, or what happened to it when one party crossed to us through the washing — not a line survives on any of it.
uses.paragraph: Whether divorce was permitted among us, and on what terms. Whether someone divorced could belong, or marry again. Whether a marriage between our own and the rival communion was even recognized as a marriage, or what happened to it when one party crossed to us through the washing — not a line survives on any of it. We would rather leave that space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.
uses.record_text:
Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians - at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it.

Is Christianity one way among many? That question was not where our energy went, and we would only be guessing if we told you our view of it. What we can tell you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently - and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.

Did we think outsiders were going to hell? We will not put words in our own mouths. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt - which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

Divorce and remarriage we cannot speak to at all. There is nothing. Whether someone divorced could belong among us, or marry again, and on what terms - not a line survives, and we would rather leave the space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

uses.sentence: The state understood perfectly well that it was the single thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.
uses.paragraph: And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. The town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Whole imperial edicts were written against that one act, which is a strange kind of compliment. The state understood perfectly well that it was the single thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.
uses.record_text:
Born again - yes, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. If you came to us from the other communion you had already been through the water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there, and we held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless, our own bishop wrote, receives not faith but guilt. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.

And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. Whole imperial edicts were written against that single act, which is a strange kind of compliment: the state understood perfectly well that it was the one thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.

Babies, or only adults choosing for themselves? We cannot tell you, and we would rather admit it than round the answer off. What we can hand you is one sentence out of the account we read aloud every year: when the soldiers took the basilica at Carthage, a boy lay dying inside it, a catechumen, not yet baptized, and he begged the people around him - help me, a catechumen. That tells you the young were among us unbaptized and waiting. It does not tell you whether infants were washed. We will not build a practice out of one dying boy.

Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Nothing survives. Money moved among us - a wealthy woman's silver bought a consecration, a bishop left the church's whole treasury with laymen and an inventory with an old woman, a fuller paid twenty pieces to be made a priest - but every one of those reaches you out of a corruption inquiry, and none of it is a rule about giving.

The end of the world we cannot speak to at all. One man among us is reported to have expounded the Apocalypse entire, taking nothing in it in a bodily sense. He is the man our own council condemned, that commentary is not among the things this telling has read, and it would be dishonest to make him our voice on the last things when we would not let him speak on anything else.

uses.sentence: There was no quiet way to do it.
uses.paragraph: And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. The town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Whole imperial edicts were written against that one act, which is a strange kind of compliment. The state understood perfectly well that it was the single thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.
uses.record_text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You asked about prayer, the meal, and fasting, and here we have to thin out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

use_note.means: Entry meant being washed on coming from the rival communion, counted as a first baptism, while discipline for wrongdoing followed no consistent rule.

a claim that a Donatist liturgy, order of service, or rule of fasting survives
a claim about the particulars of the forced-entry charges
a claim that a surviving rule explains why some condemned clergy were received back and others not

uses.paragraph: We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on - no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. What we can hand you instead is one day. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

uses.sentence: How a man came to hold it involved both the people and the bishops, and we can show you what that looked like when it went wrong.
uses.paragraph: How a man came to hold it involved both the people and the bishops, and we can show you what that looked like when it went wrong. At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. So a crowd could be overridden. It could not be ignored.
uses.record_text:
Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. It is what our people said to each other, in a letter, to readers who were likely to be next - and you should hear it as that, and not as a teaching about suffering that we ever worked out.

Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage - her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence.

use_note.means: Donatist bishops' own letters hushed a true charge, leavers were treated inconsistently, and suffering was narrated rather than explained.
not_for: a claim that any Donatist woman left a text or spoke in her own defence
a claim about what Lucilla's authority cost her
a claim that the Donatists worked out a teaching about suffering
a claim about what the Donatists wished to tell the dissenter they cut off

uses.sentence: Whatever else that tells you about us, it tells you the line was not always where our hardest language put it.
uses.paragraph: And the door was wider than our reputation. Three hundred and ten of our bishops met at Bagai and condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked men whose bodies could not find burial — and then took two of those same condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. Whatever else that tells you about us, it tells you the line was not always where our hardest language put it.
uses.record_text:
This is a real, unresolved tension. It has two truly distinct poles, and they are separated in actual institutions.
On one side stands the stated, absolute rule. Clergy who were schismatic or invalidly ordained must be rebaptized and reordained. This rule comes from the purity doctrine and from rebaptism as the rite that marks the boundary.
On the other side stands what the main Donatist party actually did. When the Maximianist clergy returned, the party received them back into office and communion. It did not repeat their ordination or their baptism.
Augustine quotes this fact directly and repeatedly, from primary material close to the Donatists. He turns it into his single central argument against their logic of rebaptism. This has been checked against his On Baptism and Answer to the Letters of Petilian.
The separation is real. This is a specific, named episode with clear limits in time. It covers the Maximianist schism of 393, its condemnation at Bagai in 394, and the reception that followed. It has its own documents: the sentences of Bagai and Cebarsussi. It is not an abstract inconsistency.
The pattern recurs in the record. What it tests, specifically, is the inner coherence of the purity doctrine. And it directly reshapes that doctrine.
Confidence is high, at this world's top evidentiary tier. Of all the tensions inside this world, this one is quoted directly most rigorously and most often across the texts we hold.
The pressure came from inside, not from any outside force. The Maximianist split (393-398) was an ongoing strain within the councils of the movement's own parallel hierarchy.
That split is the only force this tension connects to. It is the narrowest link of any pattern in this world's account. The narrowness is not a sign of doubt about our confidence. The Circumcellion pattern is different: there, a narrowing of scope does raise that doubt.
This tension is tightly scoped to one episode. Its whole evidence base is the Maximianist affair. So one connected force is exactly what we should expect. It is not a gap.
It reshapes three patterns. First, it reshapes the purity doctrine. Receiving the Maximianists without reordination strikes directly at the doctrine's inner consistency, and Augustine makes that his central argument. Second, it tests and complicates rebaptism in the same direct way. Third, it reshapes the parallel hierarchy. The split happened inside the hierarchy's own councils. It could not have happened without an institution that complex to break apart.
It has a narrow reinforcing link to the Circumcellions. Circumcellions were reportedly involved in suppressing the Maximianists. But that report comes through hostile sources. It is not treated as independent proof of what the Circumcellions were like.
It has no demonstrated link to this world's other tension: principled refusal of the state against pragmatic turns to it. The reason is the same one given there. The two work on different axes. One concerns relations with the state. The other concerns consistency of discipline inside the church. No evidence in this world's record connects them directly. Naming that absence is itself a finding, not an oversight.

use_note.means: The stated rule that invalid clergy be rebaptized and reordained stands against the Donatist mainstream's unrepeated reception of returning Maximianist clergy, in one dated episode.
not_for: a claim that the tension is an abstract inconsistency rather than a specific dated episode
a claim that the tension was driven by an outside imperial force

uses.paragraph: Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them. Some mark that can be seen from outside.
uses.record_text:
What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

use_note.means: Donatists read scripture for a visible mark of the true church, finding it in the church the world hates.
not_for: a claim about the whole community's habit of reading beyond the one 411 exchange
a claim about what the Donatists thought of the violence in scripture

uses.sentence: They sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church.
uses.paragraph: No. That is the wrong picture of us entirely. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels. They sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church.
uses.record_text:
Did the empire change what the church was? That is not a question to us. That is our whole case, and we are the party that answered yes.

Catacombs first, because it is the wrong picture. Nobody among us hid underground. The persecutions in our own time did not send us into tunnels; they sent soldiers into our buildings in broad daylight, under orders, to enforce a single church. We read the account of one such day aloud every year: a basilica at Carthage seized, a house of prayer turned into a place of feasting and licence, people clubbed to death where they knelt with their eyes shut, and buried inside the walls because there was nowhere else and nobody to stop it. That is what persecution looked like for us. Not hiding. Being visited.

Now Constantine. We petitioned him, in the first year, through his own governor - we asked him to take the matter up. He gave us a hearing at Rome and then a council at Arles, and both ruled against us, and we refused both. Not because a council cannot rule. Because a court convened, staffed and enforced by a power that has already decided which side is the church is not the church judging itself. Our own bishop is remembered putting it to the emperor's commissioners in five words: what has the Emperor to do with the Church? You should know that the only man who wrote that sentence down was one of our enemies, and he set it in a paragraph about our bishop's pride and his fits of temper. We would keep the sentence and drop the paragraph. He would say we are being selective. We would say he was there to make us look mad.

We will not pretend we were clean about this. Three times we used the same machinery we denied had standing: when we asked Constantine for judges, when we asked a later emperor for our confiscated basilicas back, and when we turned the imperial law against heretics onto our own breakaway party. We did not hide any of it. It sits in the same texts that state the doctrine at its hardest.

What did our neighbours say about us? That we washed people twice. That our country members were violent wanderers. That we were the party of a man rather than the church of Christ - and one of our own petitions, signed by our own bishops, gave them that phrase to use. And to outsiders, the strangest thing of all: two of every office in every town, two bishops, two altars, two names for the same God, and not one point of doctrine between them.

use_note.means: Donatists held that imperial favour had changed the church and refused state-convened rulings, while three times seeking imperial help themselves.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists hid in catacombs
a claim that Donatus's retort survives other than in Optatus's hostile framing
a claim that the charges of Circumcellion violence are settled fact
a claim that the Donatists never used imperial machinery

uses.paragraph: One man among us, Tyconius, did work out a system for reading Scripture — seven rules, carefully thought through. But our own council condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. Beyond that one case, we did not build a school of interpretation or a body of teachers who argued doctrine the way we argued the purity of a minister's hand.

uses.sentence: Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.
uses.paragraph: We held the scriptures as our measure, but the argument we actually made runs through Carthage, not through a doctrine of scripture alone. When we defended our practice of washing people who came to us from the rival church, we were not standing on a proof-text. We were standing on a council — eighty-seven African bishops sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that what is given outside the true church confers nothing. We thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can measure how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.
uses.record_text:
No, and the evidence for that is what our opponents had to say to beat us. Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge - wheat and tares against the world that does not know him - and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Genesis as a question about how the world was made - no. We have to tell you that nothing survives from us on it at all. That was not our fight, and we will not invent a position in it.

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

At Cirta, when Silvanus was being made bishop, the people shouted back — let it be another; hear us, God — and he was made bishop anyway, and a court heard about it years later from a man who said, I myself fought against his being made bishop. Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. It is what our people said to each other, in a letter, to readers who were likely to be next - and you should hear it as that, and not as a teaching about suffering that we ever worked out.

Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage - her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence.

uses.sentence: No child of ours speaks.
uses.paragraph: We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

uses.paragraph: What belonging cost is not one thing, and we can put figures on part of it. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale — and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives. And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. If you are far from everyone you love, that is what we would have offered you - not a feeling of connection, but a date, and a thing that happens on it whether you are there or not.

uses.sentence: So the thing being examined at our font was never your record.
uses.paragraph: The step itself is the washing. That is not a threshold you clear before belonging. It is the entry. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. We would not call it a second baptism. On our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.
uses.record_text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You asked about prayer, the meal, and fasting, and here we have to thin out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

uses.sentence: Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.
uses.paragraph: And we never wrote a book on the question either. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.
uses.record_text:
What did we argue about among ourselves? Two things, and we lost badly at both.

The first was a broken election. In 393 a deacon named Maximian was made a rival primate against our own man at Carthage - which was, if you look at it squarely, the same act our founders had once performed against Caecilian. A council of three hundred and ten of ours met at Bagai and condemned his party in language about shipwrecked bodies that could not so much as find burial. Then it took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We enforced our hard rule outward and suspended it once inward, and nobody who was in that room left an explanation.

The second was a book. Tyconius, a layman of ours, argued from Scripture - at length, and too well to be waved off - that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off, and was never taken back. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us.

Now, what did we believe about God? Here is where you will find us poorer than you expect. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

You ask what we meant by the heart. The word we actually leaned on was conscientia - a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

use_note.means: The Donatists' documented internal quarrels were the Maximianist schism, closed at Bagai, and the silencing of Tyconius over the church's extent.

One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

uses.sentence: What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient.
uses.paragraph: What we can give you is the shape of the entrance, and the doctrine that held it. Entry to us was one act: the washing. We did not think of it as baptizing twice. A hand out of a broken line washes nothing at all, so what you received from us was the first real baptism you had ever had. And we examined the giver's conscience, not yours. What we look for is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. So if you came to us unable to make your own mind hold still, the question we asked was not whether you believed steadily enough to deserve the water. The question was whether the hand offering it to you was clean.

uses.sentence: Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.
uses.paragraph: You ask about doctrine, and here the answer thins out. We were not a doctrinal movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead. The one time someone among us built an actual system for reading Scripture - Tyconius, his seven rules worked out and written down - our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.
uses.record_text:
What did we argue about among ourselves? Two things, and we lost badly at both.

The first was a broken election. In 393 a deacon named Maximian was made a rival primate against our own man at Carthage - which was, if you look at it squarely, the same act our founders had once performed against Caecilian. A council of three hundred and ten of ours met at Bagai and condemned his party in language about shipwrecked bodies that could not so much as find burial. Then it took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We enforced our hard rule outward and suspended it once inward, and nobody who was in that room left an explanation.

The second was a book. Tyconius, a layman of ours, argued from Scripture - at length, and too well to be waved off - that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off, and was never taken back. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us.

Now, what did we believe about God? Here is where you will find us poorer than you expect. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

You ask what we meant by the heart. The word we actually leaned on was conscientia - a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

use_note.means: The Donatists' documented internal quarrels were the Maximianist schism, closed at Bagai, and the silencing of Tyconius over the church's extent.
not_for: a claim that a Donatist account of either internal quarrel survives
a claim that the Donatists defined conscientia as the heart
a claim that the Donatists produced a school of theology

uses.sentence: They wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles.
uses.paragraph: The authority a bishop carried was real, but it was not absolute. When a charge came against one of our bishops, others among our own leadership wrote urging him to settle it quietly before the flame burst out — and one of those letters admits the accusation was true. They wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of those letters ends the same way: let no one learn of it. So authority among us was exercised as much in hushing things as in settling them, and we would not pretend that was rare.
uses.record_text:
Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. It is what our people said to each other, in a letter, to readers who were likely to be next - and you should hear it as that, and not as a teaching about suffering that we ever worked out.

Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage - her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing - whose hand may give what the church gives - and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

Your third we would not have understood at all. My personal Lord and Savior - the words are yours and not ours, and they carry a whole way of being a Christian we did not have: one person, deciding privately, for himself. Ours was the opposite motion. You were baptized into a body, by named hands, in a town where everyone could see which building you walked into. If you had asked one of us whether Christ was his personally, he would probably have answered by telling you whose church he belonged to. He would not have been changing the subject. To us that was the subject.

Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above. This is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. If you are far from everyone you love, that is what we would have offered you - not a feeling of connection, but a date, and a thing that happens on it whether you are there or not.

uses.sentence: Scripture told us what the church is.
uses.paragraph: And there is a second authority we cannot separate from the first: the martyrs themselves. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway. A bishop wrote to his own congregation about two of their number tortured to death, whose bodies the proconsul sank in the sea so no one could venerate them — and the sea gave them back. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them. Scripture told us what the church is. The martyrs showed us.
uses.record_text:
Before anything about how we read them: notice what they were. Objects. Heavy ones. A magistrate could demand that a bishop carry them out of a building and hand them over, and some bishops did, and the whole of us exists because of that. No other church in the empire had its scriptures turn into the exact thing that split it.

How did we read them? Combatively, and about one subject. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse - the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. That is our reading in one exchange. We went to the text for a test of which of two visible churches was the true one, and we found the church described as the party the world hates rather than the party it favours.

We will not pretend that was a method. It was not. One man among us built an actual system for reading - seven rules, worked out and written down - and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

Which books did we treat as scripture? We cannot give you a list. Nothing that survives from us settles it, and we would rather say so than hand you the canon of some other church and put our name on it.

How did someone who could not read receive any of it? By standing still and listening, on a fixed day, in a particular place. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

use_note.means: Scripture was first a surrendered object, was read combatively to identify the true church, and reached most believers by being heard aloud.

uses.paragraph: But here is where your question turns. We never had a doctrinal dispute to settle. We put everything we had into that, and we had nothing left over. We wrote no book on whether a baby is born guilty. We wrote none on what the bread becomes. We wrote none on faith set against works. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors — one book, by one man, whom we silenced.

uses.sentence: You say again; we say for the first time.
uses.paragraph: What we can hand you is small. Our own bishop said what matters is the conscience of the giver. That is a claim about the priest, not about the recipient's condition before the washing. Born again — yes, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again; we say for the first time. But that is about whose hand can give a real baptism at all, not about what guilt a person carries from birth.
uses.record_text:
Born again - yes, and we would fight you over the arithmetic. You say again. We say for the first time. If you came to us from the other communion you had already been through the water once, with words said over you and witnesses standing there, and we held that nothing whatever had happened, because the hand that did it came out of a broken line. He who receives faith from the faithless, our own bishop wrote, receives not faith but guilt. So we did not wash you a second time. We washed you.

And it was a real crossing, not a way of describing a change of heart. It happened once, on a day you could name, in front of people who could see which building you had walked into, and afterwards you were in one church and out of another. Whole imperial edicts were written against that single act, which is a strange kind of compliment: the state understood perfectly well that it was the one thing we did that made the peace it wanted impossible.

Babies, or only adults choosing for themselves? We cannot tell you, and we would rather admit it than round the answer off. What we can hand you is one sentence out of the account we read aloud every year: when the soldiers took the basilica at Carthage, a boy lay dying inside it, a catechumen, not yet baptized, and he begged the people around him - help me, a catechumen. That tells you the young were among us unbaptized and waiting. It does not tell you whether infants were washed. We will not build a practice out of one dying boy.

Did we tithe, and how did we decide what to give? Nothing survives. Money moved among us - a wealthy woman's silver bought a consecration, a bishop left the church's whole treasury with laymen and an inventory with an old woman, a fuller paid twenty pieces to be made a priest - but every one of those reaches you out of a corruption inquiry, and none of it is a rule about giving.

The end of the world we cannot speak to at all. One man among us is reported to have expounded the Apocalypse entire, taking nothing in it in a bodily sense. He is the man our own council condemned, that commentary is not among the things this telling has read, and it would be dishonest to make him our voice on the last things when we would not let him speak on anything else.

use_note.means: Donatists counted the washing of those coming from the rival communion as a first baptism, a public act imperial law targeted.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists baptized infants, or that they did not
a claim about Donatist rules of giving or tithing
a claim about Donatist teaching on the end of the world

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.
